Water Hunt on Mars

  1. Follow the rover (on by default): after you press Drill, the camera rides with the rover to the square, then moves in close as the arm unfolds and the drill goes in, with a cutaway of the layers beside it. Press Skip to hurry it along, or turn Follow the rover off in the Briefing panel.
  2. Pick a mission from Mission control. You are the mission scientist: a rover, a handful of probes and a map. Nothing tells you where the water is. The numbers and the ground do.
  3. Look at the map. Each square is one kind of ground, and the names are never shown during a mission. Learn to tell them apart by eye.
  4. Probe: tap a square, then press Drill (or Enter). The rover drives there and drills. You get a number (how much of the soil sample is water, by weight) and a one-word description of the soil. The word is sometimes wrong.
  5. From Mission 2 you choose the drill depth. Deeper drilling costs more time.
  6. Orbiter passes (Missions 2 and 3): choose Neutron pass and tap a square to scan the 3 × 3 block around it, or Radar line to scan a whole row. They are cheaper than a probe but coarser.
  7. A water zone is ice-rich ground (15% water or more) within 1 m of the surface. It lights up when a probe reads it. Find them all before you run out of probes (or, in Mission 3, daylight).
  8. Switch views at any time (keys 1–4): the Map, the Arm camera (the drill and a cutaway of the layers), the Orbiter and the Sun dial.
  9. The debrief shows the whole hidden map, your path, the terrain names, how informative each probe was, and the real missions. Then open the Lab Bench to turn every knob, or World Hop to see the same ground on another world or in another era.
  10. Challenges in Mission control: race the rival bot, the daily map, a fresh impact, a dust storm, Mystery World, and Mission Control for two players.

Rover model: Perseverance, NASA/JPL-Caltech (NASA 3D Resources).

  • A small reading is not zero water: ordinary soil holds 1 to 3% water by weight, bound in its grains.
  • Depth matters: ice sits below an ice table. A drill that stops above it reads dry even right over ice.
  • Why ice sits where it does: ice survives where the ground stays colder than the frost point. Every 6 K warmer lets about e (2.7) times more vapour escape, so the ice table sinks fast as the ground warms.
  • Shade and slope: pole-facing slopes and shadowed crater floors are colder, so ice sits shallower there.
  • Minerals or ice: 6 to 12% with a clayey soil is water locked in minerals, and its neighbours do not rise.
  • Patterns: readings near a zone rise in a halo, so probing beside a rising reading usually pays. It stops working when the halo is narrow or the ground type changes.
  • Remote sensing: hydrogen slows neutrons, so wetter ground returns fewer. Orbit sees averages; the ground confirms.
  • Evidence: update your belief after every reading, and judge which probe would have taught you the most.
  • Worlds: tilt, temperature, vapour and era move the water. "Water-rich" depends on the world.
